body.name: Congenital bile acid synthesis defect type 2

text.html:
Congenital bile acid synthesis defect type 2 is a disorder that impairs the production and flow of a digestive fluid called bile. Bile is made and released by the liver. People with congenital bile acid synthesis defect 2 have trouble making an important component of bile called bile acids. Bile acids stimulate bile flow and help the body absorb fats and fat-soluble vitamins, such as vitamins A, D, E, and K.

Although the specific signs and symptoms can vary among affected individuals, the features of congenital bile acid synthesis defect type 2 are often present at birth (congenital) or develop during infancy and can include:

• Impaired flow of bile from the liver (cholestasis)
• Yellowing of the skin and the whites of the eyes (jaundice)
• An enlarged liver (hepatomegaly)
• An inability to grow and gain weight at the expected rate (faltering weight)
• Excess fat in the feces (steatorrhea)

As the condition progresses, individuals with congenital bile acid synthesis defect type 2 may also develop:

• A softening and weakening of the bones (rickets)
• Blood clotting problems that may lead to prolonged bleeding
• Inflammation of the liver (hepatitis)

If left untreated, congenital bile acid synthesis defect type 2 often leads to chronic liver disease (cirrhosis) and liver failure in childhood. However, early diagnosis and appropriate treatment can improve liver function and prevent further damage.
